24.text:
Advertisements now appear on screens, streets and phones, and many feel that advertising harms traditional values. I agree to some extent, since advertising can weaken traditional values by promoting consumption, although it is not the only influence on society.

To begin with, advertising can weaken traditional values. Adverts that link happiness to buying and that use foreign lifestyles can displace modest habits and family customs. A campaign that shows a perfect life as one with the latest phone and fashionable clothes, for example, may persuade young people that status matters more than modesty or respect for elders. Traditional values such as saving money, repairing old things and sharing with relatives can seem old-fashioned when advertisers present constant consumption as normal. Children who grow up with such messages often put pressure on their parents to buy brands, which strains family budgets and relationships.

However, advertising is not the only force that changes values, and it can sometimes support them. Some campaigns celebrate local festivals, family reunions and national crafts, and they make traditions visible to a wide audience. A holiday advert that shows several generations eating together, for example, reminds viewers of the importance of family. Values also change through education, migration, travel and the internet, so that blaming advertising alone is unfair. Governments can reduce the harm by setting standards on honesty and by encouraging adverts which respect local culture, while families and schools teach critical thinking about commercial messages.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that advertising harms traditional values, particularly by encouraging materialism, but its influence should not be exaggerated.

26.text:
Millions of people check their phones many times a day to see messages and photographs from friends, and some claim that social media causes loneliness. I agree to a limited extent, since social media can increase loneliness when it replaces real contact, but it also connects isolated people.

To begin with, social media can increase loneliness when it replaces face-to-face contact. Hours of scrolling reduce time spent with real friends and invite unhealthy comparison. A teenager who spends every evening looking at pictures of friends at parties, for example, may feel excluded and conclude that her own life is dull. Fear of missing out is a common feeling, and counting likes can make users anxious about their popularity. Online friendships are often shallow, since people share only the best moments and rarely talk about real worries, so that users may have hundreds of contacts yet nobody to confide in. Several studies have linked heavy use with depression and lower life satisfaction.

However, social media can also reduce isolation. Online groups help the housebound, migrants and people with rare interests to find friends. An elderly woman who cannot leave her flat, for example, can chat with grandchildren on video and join a discussion group for her hobbies. People who live abroad can stay in touch with their families, and those who are shy may find it easier to start conversations online and then meet in person. The effect therefore depends on how it is used: as a complement to real relationships, social media can be helpful, while as a substitute it is harmful. Setting limits on screen time and prioritising real meetings can protect users.

In conclusion, social media causes loneliness only to a limited extent, and its effect depends on how people use it.

44.text:
Young people follow singers, footballers and film stars on screens every day, and many feel that celebrities have a negative influence on them. I agree to some extent, since some celebrities set a poor example, although others have a very positive influence.

To begin with, celebrities can set a negative example for young fans. Young people imitate stars who display luxury, extreme diets or reckless behaviour. A teenager who sees an idol spend huge sums on fashion and cars, for example, may feel that happiness depends on money and may try to copy that lifestyle. Pictures of unnaturally thin models and edited bodies can lead to dissatisfaction with appearance and eating problems, and scandals involving drugs, alcohol or violence may make such behaviour seem acceptable. Because fans often look up to their idols, they may defend their actions or follow their habits without thinking about the consequences. Many stars also promote products in return for payment, which encourages young people to buy things they do not need.

However, many celebrities inspire positive habits. Athletes and artists who work hard, give to charity or speak about mental health encourage young people to do the same. A footballer who grew up in poverty and now funds schools, for example, shows what discipline and generosity can achieve. Musicians who talk openly about their own struggles help fans to feel less alone, and actors who support environmental campaigns raise awareness among their followers. The influence therefore depends on which role models are promoted. Parents and teachers can help by discussing the lives of public figures critically and by drawing attention to those who offer genuine examples.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that celebrities can influence young people negatively, but the overall effect depends on the example that they set.

64.text:
Readers once relied on newspapers and television bulletins, but today many get their information from websites and social networks, and many feel that traditional media is less trustworthy than online sources. I disagree with this view, since traditional media usually checks facts and carries legal responsibility, although it is not perfect.

To begin with, traditional media is usually more reliable than online sources. Editors verify stories and can be held accountable, while anyone can post online without checking. A national newspaper that publishes a false claim, for example, risks legal action and loss of reputation, so reporters need two or more sources before printing. Professional journalists are trained in ethics, and newsrooms have procedures for corrections. Many online sources, in contrast, are anonymous, funded by advertising that rewards shocking headlines, or created to spread a political message. Fake stories travel faster than corrections on social platforms, and users often share content without reading it.

However, traditional media is not free from faults. It can be biased by owners or political leanings, it may be slow to react to events, and it sometimes ignores topics that do not interest its main audience. Online sources have advantages: they are fast, offer diverse views and allow ordinary people to record events that official media overlook. Some independent websites and blogs provide excellent analysis. Readers should therefore compare several sources, check who is responsible for a report and look for evidence. Schools can teach media literacy so that young people learn to distinguish reliable from unreliable information.

In conclusion, I disagree that traditional media is less trustworthy than online sources, although readers should always use several sources and think critically.

A holiday photograph with perfect light, a smiling family and a spotless home appears in thousands of feeds every day, and many feel that photos and posts on social media are misleading. I agree with this view, since people edit and select what they show, although some posts are honest.

To begin with, photos and posts on social media are often misleading because people edit and select what they show. Filters, editing and carefully chosen moments create flawless images of life. A young woman who spends an hour taking fifty pictures before posting the best one, for example, may use filters to change her skin and shape, so that the result differs greatly from reality. People share holidays, promotions and celebrations, but rarely mention arguments, failures and ordinary days. Influencers may also be paid to praise products without admitting that they have not used them, and some staged scenes are presented as spontaneous.

Furthermore, these images affect viewers. Those who see only perfect lives compare themselves unfairly and feel dissatisfied with their own appearance, income or relationships. Teenagers are especially vulnerable, since they are still forming their identity, and research has linked heavy use with anxiety and low self-esteem. However, not all posts are dishonest, and many people use the platforms to share real experiences, news and creative work. Media literacy and honest labelling reduce the harm. Schools can teach students how images are edited, platforms can require labels on altered or sponsored photographs, and users can remind themselves that online lives are selected highlights.

In conclusion, I agree that many photos and posts on social media are misleading, but education and clear labelling can help people to view them more critically.

plan.think: Mở bài nêu bức ảnh kỳ nghỉ hoàn hảo; agree.

Chỉnh sửa và chọn lọc: bộ lọc, khoảnh khắc chọn tạo hình ảnh hoàn hảo; ví dụ cô gái chụp 50 ảnh một giờ chọn một, dùng bộ lọc đổi da, dáng khác hẳn thực; chia sẻ kỳ nghỉ, thăng chức, ít cãi vã, thất bại; người ảnh hưởng được trả khen sản phẩm chưa dùng; cảnh dàn dựng như tự nhiên.

Ảnh hưởng người xem: so sánh không công bằng, không hài lòng ngoại hình, thu nhập, quan hệ; thiếu niên dễ tổn thương, nghiên cứu liên hệ lo âu; nhưng không phải bài nào cũng giả; hiểu biết truyền thông, nhãn trung thực; trường dạy cách chỉnh ảnh, nền tảng yêu cầu nhãn ảnh chỉnh, tài trợ.
Agree; giáo dục, dán nhãn giúp nhìn phê phán.

86.text:
Every year, popular novels are turned into films, and people often debate which form is better, so that the statement that books are better than films raises a lively question. I agree to a large extent, although films have strengths of their own.

To begin with, books develop imagination and language more deeply. Reading requires readers to picture scenes, builds vocabulary and allows detailed ideas. A reader of a long novel, for example, imagines the faces, voices and places in his own way, and meets sentences and words that he would rarely hear in conversation. Books allow access to the inner thoughts of characters, which films can only suggest, and they can explore complicated arguments, history and science in great depth. Reading also improves concentration and writing skills, and it is a portable and cheap hobby that can be enjoyed anywhere. Studies suggest that regular readers have larger vocabularies and better understanding of others.

However, films give vivid and emotional experiences quickly. They combine images, music and acting to deliver a story in two hours, which suits people who have little time. A film adaptation of a classic, for example, can introduce a story to those who would never open the book, and spectacular scenes such as battles or landscapes are more powerful on screen. Films can also be watched with friends and discussed afterwards. Therefore, each form has its strengths, and the best choice depends on purpose: for deep learning, language and reflection, books are superior, while for entertainment and shared experience, films are often more convenient.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that books are better than films, but both have an important place in culture.

plan.think: Mở bài nêu tiểu thuyết nổi tiếng được chuyển thể; largely agree.

Sách phát triển trí tưởng tượng, ngôn ngữ sâu hơn: tưởng tượng cảnh, từ vựng, ý chi tiết; ví dụ người đọc tiểu thuyết dài tưởng tượng mặt, giọng, nơi theo cách riêng, gặp câu từ ít nghe; nội tâm nhân vật; lập luận phức tạp, lịch sử, khoa học; tập trung, viết; rẻ; từ vựng, thấu hiểu.

Phim sống động, cảm xúc nhanh: hình ảnh, nhạc, diễn xuất, hai giờ; ví dụ chuyển thể kinh điển giới thiệu cho người không mở sách, cảnh chiến đấu, phong cảnh; xem với bạn thảo luận; tuỳ mục đích: học sâu thì sách, giải trí và trải nghiệm chung thì phim.
Sách tốt hơn ở mức lớn; cả hai quan trọng.

104.text:
Cartoon characters, free toys and bright colours fill many programmes and websites that children watch, and many feel that adverts target children inappropriately. I agree with this view, since young children cannot judge persuasion, although some advertising can be harmless.

To begin with, advertising aimed at children is unfair because they cannot judge persuasion. Young children do not understand that adverts sell, so cartoon characters and games lead them to demand toys and sugary snacks. A six-year-old who sees a favourite character on a cereal box, for example, believes that the product is special and will repeat the request until her parents agree. Children do not have the experience to evaluate claims or to resist pressure, and psychologists say that before the age of eight they take messages at face value. Advertisers also use tricks such as competitions, collectable items and websites that blend games with promotions to make children want the brand.

Furthermore, such advertising has harmful effects. It pressures parents who must refuse again and again, and it encourages materialism and unhealthy habits, because many adverts promote sweets, fast food and expensive toys. Children who cannot have the latest fashion may feel left out, which damages their self-esteem. However, not all advertising to children is harmful, and some promotes books, sports or educational games. Strict rules are nevertheless justified: governments can ban manipulative techniques, limit adverts during children's programmes, require clear labelling of promotions and restrict the promotion of unhealthy food. Parents and schools should also teach children how advertising works.

In conclusion, I agree that adverts target children inappropriately, and stricter regulation would protect them.

115.text:
Posters for burgers, sweets and fizzy drinks surround children on screens and streets, and some believe that governments should limit advertising of unhealthy food. I agree to a large extent, since such advertising shapes children's choices and fuels obesity, although education must go with it.

To begin with, governments should restrict advertising of unhealthy food because it shapes children's choices. Repeated adverts for sweets and fast food make them attractive and normal. A child who sees a burger advertised during every cartoon, for example, will ask for it, and food companies spend huge sums on this because it works. Obesity and type two diabetes are rising rapidly among young people, which costs health services billions and shortens lives. Experiments show that children who watch such adverts eat more snacks immediately afterwards. Limiting broadcast times and locations reduces demand, and countries that have banned such advertising before nine in the evening or near schools have recorded reductions in the purchase of unhealthy products.

However, advertising limits alone are not sufficient, and they raise questions about freedom of trade. Companies argue that their products are legal and that consumers are responsible for their own choices. Parents also have a role in shaping habits at home. Education should therefore accompany restrictions: schools can teach nutrition and cooking, labelling can show sugar and fat clearly, and healthy food should be made cheaper and easier to find. Taxes on sugary drinks have also encouraged manufacturers to reduce sugar. When these measures are combined, public health costs fall and children grow up with better habits.

In conclusion, I agree that governments should limit the advertising of unhealthy food, as long as this is part of a wider strategy for healthy living.

Chỉ hạn chế chưa đủ, đụng tự do thương mại: công ty cho là hợp pháp, người tiêu dùng chịu trách nhiệm; cha mẹ; giáo dục: dinh dưỡng, nấu ăn, nhãn đường, chất béo, đồ lành mạnh rẻ; thuế nước ngọt; chi phí y tế giảm.

120.text:
Posts, videos and comments spread across social platforms in seconds, and the question is to what extent governments should regulate social media content. I believe that governments should regulate illegal and harmful content, but they should avoid censoring legitimate opinion.

To begin with, governments should regulate content that is clearly illegal or harmful. Platforms spread hate speech, threats and content harmful to children, so laws can demand quick removal. A video that encourages violence against a minority group, for example, can lead to real attacks if it is shared widely, and companies may not act unless they face penalties. Material such as child abuse images, terrorist propaganda and fraud is already illegal offline, and there is no reason why it should be tolerated online. Governments can also require platforms to protect young users, to publish reports on the removal of harmful posts and to give users ways to complain. Without regulation, companies tend to put profit before safety.

However, vague or excessive rules allow officials to silence critics, and freedom of expression is a basic right. A law that bans posts that insult the government, for example, could be used to punish journalists and opponents. Opinions that are unpopular or offensive to some people are not necessarily harmful, and open debate helps societies to find the truth. Clear, narrow rules, with independent oversight and the right to appeal, protect both safety and freedom. Platforms should also be transparent about how their algorithms and moderation work. Cooperation between governments, companies and civil society is more effective than control by the state alone.

In conclusion, governments should regulate social media content to a moderate extent, concentrating on illegal and clearly harmful material while protecting freedom of speech.

Nội dung rõ ràng bất hợp pháp hoặc có hại: thù hận, đe doạ, hại trẻ nên luật đòi gỡ nhanh; ví dụ video kích động bạo lực nhắm thiểu số dẫn tấn công thật; công ty không hành động nếu không bị phạt; hình ảnh lạm dụng trẻ, tuyên truyền khủng bố, lừa đảo đã bất hợp pháp ngoài đời; bảo vệ người dùng trẻ, báo cáo gỡ, khiếu nại; không điều tiết lợi nhuận trước an toàn.

Điều tiết mức vừa phải, tập trung nội dung bất hợp pháp và có hại.

134.text:
A cruel message, a humiliating photograph or a false rumour can reach a whole school within minutes, and many people think that social networks increase cyberbullying. I agree with this view, since abuse can be anonymous, constant and public, although bullying also exists offline.

To begin with, social networks increase cyberbullying because abuse can be anonymous, constant and public. Bullies can reach victims at any hour and share insults with a large audience, so harm spreads quickly and is hard to escape. A girl who is mocked by classmates in a group chat, for example, may receive messages late at night in her own bedroom, where she once felt safe. Offensive comments and edited pictures can be copied and shared endlessly, and they can remain online for years. Anonymous accounts remove the fear of being identified, which makes some people far crueller than they would be in person, and observers often join in without thinking.

Furthermore, the consequences can be severe. Victims often suffer anxiety, depression and loss of sleep, perform worse at school and, in tragic cases, harm themselves. However, bullying existed long before the internet, and some of it still takes place in classrooms and playgrounds. Social networks have not created cruelty; they have given it new tools and a larger audience. Platforms, schools and parents must therefore act together. Platforms should make it easy to report abuse, remove harmful posts quickly and block repeat offenders, schools should teach students how to behave online and how to support victims, and parents should talk openly with their children and keep an eye on warning signs.

In conclusion, I agree that social networks increase cyberbullying, and effective protection requires cooperation between technology companies, schools and families.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: mạng xã hội tăng bắt nạt trực tuyến — agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu tin nhắn độc ác, ảnh làm nhục, tin đồn lan cả trường; agree.

Lạm dụng ẩn danh, liên tục, công khai: bắt nạt tiếp cận nạn nhân mọi giờ, chia sẻ với khán giả lớn; ví dụ cô gái bị bạn chế giễu trong nhóm chat nhận tin muộn trong phòng ngủ an toàn; bình luận, ảnh chỉnh sao chép chia sẻ mãi, tồn tại nhiều năm; tài khoản ẩn danh mất sợ bị nhận ra; người xem hùa theo.

Nạn nhân lo âu, trầm cảm, mất ngủ, học kém, trường hợp bi thảm tự hại; nhưng bắt nạt có từ trước, vẫn ở lớp học, sân chơi; mạng xã hội cho công cụ mới và khán giả lớn; nền tảng báo cáo dễ, gỡ nhanh, chặn người lặp lại; trường dạy ứng xử; cha mẹ trò chuyện, để ý dấu hiệu.
Agree; cần hợp tác.
